transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-06-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Alex Moran, Priya Nair, Sam Cho (Redwood) — Marta Ruiz, Daniel Park, Eve Sinclair, James O'Leary (Lumina)
Shared artifacts: demo deck (link: drive.redwood/demo-lumina), validation spreadsheet (link: drive.lumina/poc-results), security pack (link: drive.redwood/security-pack.pdf)

Summary:
- Weekly POC sync focusing on integration patterns for SDK usage, tool/function calling, and validating structured output for Lumina's clinical note ingestion flows.
- Action items agreed: SDK snippet, validation runs, JSON schema examples, benchmarking slots.

Topics: SDK patterns, function-calling edge cases, structured JSON outputs, latency vs batching tradeoffs, error handling, safety/signature verification, security questions.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep to 45 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Marta: Hi, Marta here.
[00:08] Daniel: Daniel — hi.
[00:09] Eve: Eve on security.
[00:11] James: James — frontend.
[00:13] Priya: Priya from Redwood SE. Sam and Alex here as well.
[00:16] Alex: Cool. Last week we pushed the initial SDK snippet and you ran the stub — Marta, can you give a quick 2-minute status?
[00:26] Marta: Sure, so we integrated the basic SDK call in our staging service. We wired tool-calling for entity extraction and a function that maps to the EHR fields. We hit a couple of gotchas — the response shape varied, so our parser errored sometimes. We also saw a few requests time out when batching was enabled in our sidecar.
[00:45] Priya: OK, that's helpful. On the response shape, did you pin a schema or are you doing schema-less parsing?
[00:52] Marta: Right now schema-less, parser is fairly brittle. We tried forcing the model to emit JSON by priming with system instruction but still got trailing text and sometimes malformed arrays.
[01:06] Sam: This is where structured-output enforcement helps — we'll share recommended system prompt + output-schema enforcement via the SDK's functions wrapper. The SDK has a validate_json helper that can run a quick JSON schema check post-response and return a structured error code.
[01:24] Daniel: Can you show an example of the SDK call we should use for the tool-calling flow? The sample in the repo was a bit thin for our orchestration code.
[01:32] Priya: Yeah, we'll upload an annotated snippet. High level: call redwood.client.generate with tools=[extract_entities_fn], functions_enable=true, include_function_responses=true. We recommend making the function signature strict — types and required fields — so the model maps directly. We'll annotate retry/backoff for 409/429s and show how to fallback to a smaller model for quick responses.
[01:54] Marta: On retries — if we retry, we worry about duplicated side effects. Our extractor writes to a staging DB.
[02:00] Alex: Good callout. For side effects, the pattern is: have the model produce only a delta or a dry-run response and let your service apply the change idempotently. We can add an example where the function returns an idempotency key and a boolean 'commit' flag.
[02:16] Eve: From security perspective, we need to ensure function-call payloads are signed/encrypted and we want to see KMS integration. Does Redwood's SDK support encryption-at-rest and KMS enforcements for private deployments?
[02:28] Priya: Yes, for Redwood Private we support customer KMS + HSM integrations. We'll attach the security pack link with details and a short diagram. For hosted flows we store minimal inputs and can redact PII at the SDK layer before payloads hit the network.
[02:45] Eve: Also need an audit trail for all function invocations.
[02:48] Sam: Console has per-route logs and trace IDs. We can show how to include correlation IDs in the SDK so every model response maps to a request in your logging system.
[02:58] James: Back to malformed JSON — sometimes the model emits an extra trailing period or says "note: check manual" appended to JSON. How do we robustly recover?
[03:08] Priya: Two options: 1) Strict function signature + use functions API so model returns structured payloads without free text, 2) Post-process with the validate_json helper + fallback to a post-hoc parser that strips trailing text. We'll provide sample code for both.
[03:24] Marta: For the clinical notes flow we need nested lists (meds -> doses -> timestamps) and sometimes the model collapses arrays into comma strings.
[03:32] Sam: Recommend forcing explicit arrays in the schema, and include examples in the system prompt. Also include negative examples for the thing you don't want. We had success with a "canonical example" technique in the last POC.
[03:49] Daniel: Can Redwood's runtime do automatic prefix caching for repeated templates? We noticed repeated tokens in our prompts for the EHR headers.
[03:57] Priya: Yes — the runtime does prefix/KV caching. Note that caching effectiveness varies with sequence length. If you have long static context, caching helps a lot. However, be careful with dynamic patient-specific prompts. We can show your team how to split static template vs variable fields to maximize cache hits.
[04:14] Marta: Interesting, we saw a "KV cash" entry in the logs earlier — I think transcription or logging typo.
[04:19] Alex: (laughs) yeah KV cache sometimes becomes KV cash in human notes.
[04:22] [05:00] Priya: Quick demonstration: I'll paste a small SDK snippet (live share) — pseudo-code:
function callExtractor(input) {
  const client = new RedwoodClient({ apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY });
  const resp = await client.generate({
    model: 'redwood-2-compact',
    messages: [...],
    tools: [extract_entities_fn],
    function_call: 'auto',
    max_tokens: 512
  });
  // handle function response, validate JSON schema 
}
[05:40] James: How do we handle streaming vs non-streaming for this? Streaming would help UI latency when generating long notes.
[05:47] Sam: We support streaming responses and function-calling streaming. For your UI use case we recommend streaming partial outputs while still buffering and validating the final structured payload. Be aware of the tradeoff: streaming increases perceived latency improvements but can complicate strict schema enforcement.
[06:08] Marta: On throughput, we run 30 requests/sec during peak in staging and want to avoid cold starts in the dedicated tests.
[06:16] Alex: For the dedicated capacity test we'll reserve a pool sized to your peak and run warm-up sequences. We'll also test two routing policies: hosted-first with dedicated fallback, and dedicated-primary. We'll measure 95p latency and token cost.
[06:32] Daniel: When you say dedicated-primary, does that route everything to our reserved pool even if underutilized?
[06:38] Priya: Yes, dedicated-primary pins your workload to the reserved GPUs; dedicated fallback means we spill to hosted when the pool is saturated. There's also autoscaling burst options.
[06:48] Eve: For compliance we need logs retained 12 months, and SAML/SSO integration — are those available?
[06:54] Sam: Yes, enterprise features include long-term log retention, SSO via SAML, RBAC, and audit exports. We'll attach the enterprise feature sheet.
[07:03] Marta: A corner-case question: tool-calling failure modes — if the model calls a tool with malformed args, can we capture the raw model output and replay it to debug?
[07:14] Priya: The SDK stores raw model responses when debug mode is on. We can surface that via the console or a debug endpoint. We'll show an example of turning on verbose logs for a single route during the POC.
[07:28] Daniel: About the validation harness — we want to run unit tests that assert exact keys and types, and then integration tests allowing small deviations. Any recommendations?
[07:37] Sam: Suggest two-layer testing: schema-level unit tests (strict) using JSON schema validator, and golden-file integration tests where you compare canonical outputs with a tolerance for reordering in arrays or tokenization noise. We'll share a small test harness repo example.
[07:56] Marta: On the subject of models — is there a recommended model family for token-cost sensitive flows?
[08:02] Priya: For structured extraction, we recommend a smaller deterministic variant (e.g., redwood-2-compact or quantized variants) with function-calling, because it reduces hallucination surface and cost. For open-ended summarization use larger models.
[08:16] James: Anything about tokenization differences? We noticed token counts are different vs our internal tokenizer.
[08:22] Sam: Tokenizers differ; we'll include a tokenization utility in the SDK that approximates platform tokens and show how to budget. Also mention that quantized runtimes may have different per-token latency characteristics.
[08:37] [10:00] Marta: We ran 200 sample queries — results are in the spreadsheet. Key failures: 18% malformed JSON, 6% missing required keys, 3% latency > 1s on compact model.
[10:16] Alex: That's very actionable. For the malformed JSON we'll provide both prompt templates and the SDK validate_json helper. For latency we should test dedicated pool and non-batched small batches — sometimes batching hurts low-latency.
[10:30] Daniel: How do we instrument to compare batching on/off?
[10:33] Priya: Use the SDK's per-request timing hooks. We'll also provide a small script that generates synthetic load with configurable batch windows and reports mean/95/99 latencies.
[10:45] Eve: About data residency — some of our patient data must stay inside EU regions. Can we pin region routing?
[10:51] Sam: Yes, routing policies support region pinning. For Private we can deploy in your VPC in EU. We'll document the network diagram and compliance checklist.
[10:59] Marta: Two small things from our engineers: 1) sample JS + Python SDKs for function-calling, 2) recommendation on using streaming for UI and non-stream for final commit.
[11:10] Priya: We'll deliver both. For JS we'll show streaming handlers that accumulate tokens into a buffer and run schema validation on completion. For Python we'll show the sync/async examples.
[11:25] James: Error codes — do you have a canonical list for 400/422/429/5xx? We saw 422 for malformed function args earlier.
[11:33] Alex: We'll include the error map in the SDK docs. 422 is malformed input, 409 is conflict, 429 rate limit, 503 transient backend. We'll note best-practice backoff jitter.
[11:45] Marta: On billed tokens — can we get token-level cost breakdowns for the flows in the console?
[11:50] Sam: Yes, Console shows token-level breakdown per-route and per-model. We can export usage by trace id for your accounting.
[11:58] Daniel: Any concerns about PII redaction that we should be aware of?
[12:02] Eve: We need assurances about redaction at the SDK layer prior to sending.
[12:06] Priya: We'll include a redaction helper that masks PHI fields before the call and an option to enforce client-side redaction in the SDK.
[12:16] [15:00] Alex: Quick demo pause — I'm going to summarize the agreed next steps so we all have the same list.
[15:08] Alex: Redwood will: 1) Share annotated SDK snippet for function-calling and streaming examples (Priya) 2) Provide structured-output examples and JSON schema (Sam) 3) Attach security pack and enterprise feature sheet (Sam) 4) Propose benchmarking times for dedicated pool tests (Alex).
[15:23] Marta: Lumina will: run validation harness on 3 flows, upload results spreadsheet, and mark critical failures.
[15:30] Daniel: We'll also confirm the IP ranges and compliance docs for our security team to review.
[15:34] Eve: We'll review the security pack and revert with any follow-ups.
[15:38] James: Small note — frontend will try streaming example next week and report UI integration issues.
[15:44] Priya: Any blockers from Redwood side?
[15:46] Alex: No blockers; just need to produce the artifacts.
[15:50] Marta: One last technical note — when you send the SDK snippet, could you include a tiny example showing how to handle partial failures in multi-tool flows? We had an occurrence where the extraction tool succeeded but the enrichment tool failed and we lost the idempotency key.
[16:02] Priya: Yes, include explicit transaction patterns: function returns {idempotency_key, status: 'dry-run'| 'commit'} and then your orchestrator writes guarded by the idempotency key. We'll add code sample.
[16:12] Alex: Great. If no further items, let's keep the cadence weekly and we'll reconvene same time next week.
[16:18] Marta: Works for us. Thanks everyone.
[16:20] Daniel: Thanks.
[16:21] Eve: Thanks.

End of transcript.
